lec05kp14-u01-p1-title.text: Four points have 16 labelings and one line separates only 14; the missing 2 are XOR

lec05kp14-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP13 lifted the data to new coordinates and then used a straight line. Does lifting really help? First count: into how many two-class splits can one line cut some points?

lec05kp14-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-dichotomy
lec05kp14-u01-p1-fig1.text: The 16 labelings of the four corners of a square: 14 green boxes are separable by one line and the 2 red boxes with diagonal pairs (XOR and XNOR) are not.

image.alt: The 16 labelings of the four corners of a square: 14 green boxes are separable by one line and the 2 red boxes with diagonal pairs (XOR and XNOR) are not.

lec05kp14-u01-p1-term:二分.name: term:Dichotomy
lec05kp14-u01-p1-term:二分.text: **Dichotomy**: one way of labeling $N$ points with two classes; the ones a line (hyperplane) can realize are the linear dichotomies.

lec05kp14-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p1-c1.text: **3 points**: all 8 labelings can be separated by a line.

lec05kp14-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp14-u01-p1-c2.text: **4 points** (corners of a square): 14 of the 16 labelings are separable; the 2 that are not put the diagonal pairs together, $[(A,D),(B,C)]$, which are XOR and its mirror XNOR (A top-left, B bottom-left, C top-right, D bottom-right; checked one by one by a program).

lec05kp14-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp14-u01-p2-title.text: Linear dichotomies are counted: O(N, l) = 2Σ C(N−1, i), i = 0 to l

lec05kp14-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p2-bridge.text: One line separates only 14 of 16 labelings, 2 are missing. Can we compute the count directly?

lec05kp14-u01-p2-term:一般位置.name: term:General position
lec05kp14-u01-p2-term:一般位置.text: **General position**: $l$-dimensional points with no $l+1$ on one $(l-1)$-dimensional hyperplane (in 2-D, no three on a line).

lec05kp14-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp14-u01-p3-title.text: With random labels the probability of separable is P = O/2^N: in two dimensions 87.5% at N=4 and half at N=6

lec05kp14-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p3-bridge.text: All labelings are separable while $N\le l+1$ and beyond that some are missing. If the labels are random, what is the probability of separable?

lec05kp14-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-prob
lec05kp14-u01-p3-fig1.text: Bar chart of the probability of separable for l=2 and N=1 to 10: 1 for the first three, 0.875 at N=4, 0.688 at N=5, exactly 0.5 at N=6, down to 0.09.

image.alt: Bar chart of the probability of separable for l=2 and N=1 to 10: 1 for the first three, 0.875 at N=4, 0.688 at N=5, exactly 0.5 at N=6, down to 0.09.

lec05kp14-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp14-u01-p3-c3.text: **Reading it**: once $N$ passes $l+1=3$ the probability starts to fall and reaches exactly half at $N=6$.

lec05kp14-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp14-u01-p4-title.text: Write N as r(l+1): every curve passes through (2, 1/2) and turns steeper with dimension

lec05kp14-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p4-bridge.text: In two dimensions $N=6$ gives exactly half. In other dimensions, where does the half appear?

lec05kp14-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-curves
lec05kp14-u01-p4-fig1.text: Probability of separable against r=N/(l+1) for l=1, 3, 7, 19 and 99: all pass through (2, 0.5) and the turn gets steeper with dimension.

image.alt: Probability of separable against r=N/(l+1) for l=1, 3, 7, 19 and 99: all pass through (2, 0.5) and the turn gets steeper with dimension.

lec05kp14-u01-p4-term:相變.name: term:Phase transition
lec05kp14-u01-p4-term:相變.text: **Phase transition**: the turn of the probability from 1 down to 0 gets sharper as the dimension grows, like water freezing; the critical point is at $r=2$.

lec05kp14-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p4-c1.text: **Critical point**: let $r=N/(l+1)$, i.e. $N=r(l+1)$; at $r=2$, i.e. $N=2(l+1)$, $O(2l+2,l)=2^{2l+1}$ so the probability is $1/2$ (checked for $l=1..7$).

lec05kp14-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp14-u01-p5-title.text: In two dimensions, random points and labels give 0.865 at N=4 and 0.503 at N=6, matching the formula

lec05kp14-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p5-bridge.text: At the critical point $r=2$ the probability is exactly $1/2$. Trying random points with random labels, do we get the same numbers?

lec05kp14-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-mc
lec05kp14-u01-p5-fig1.text: Formula against the 1500-run simulation: 0.875 against 0.865 at N=4 and 0.500 against 0.503 at N=6.

image.alt: Formula against the 1500-run simulation: 0.875 against 0.865 at N=4 and 0.500 against 0.503 at N=6.

lec05kp14-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p5-c1.text: **Method**: each run draws $N$ two-dimensional Gaussian points with random $\pm1$ labels and uses a linear program to decide whether a separating line exists; 1500 runs each.

lec05kp14-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp14-u01-p5-c3.text: **Error**: with 1500 runs the standard error is about 0.01, so the gap is about one standard error.

lec05kp14-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp14-u01-p6-title.text: Quadratic features lift the probability of separable random labels from 0.49 to 1.00

lec05kp14-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p6-bridge.text: The simulation matches the formula: in two dimensions $N=6$ is only 0.5. What about the same points after lifting?

lec05kp14-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-lift
lec05kp14-u01-p6-fig1.text: Fraction of separable random labelings of N=6 random points: 0.494 in the original two dimensions and 1.000 with quadratic features (5 dimensions).

image.alt: Fraction of separable random labelings of N=6 random points: 0.494 in the original two dimensions and 1.000 with quadratic features (5 dimensions).

lec05kp14-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p6-c1.text: **Method**: the same random points and labels; $[x_1,x_2]$ is $l=2$ and adding $x_1^2,x_2^2,x_1x_2$ makes $l=5$.

lec05kp14-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp14-u01-p6-c2.text: **Formula prediction**: $N=6\le l+1=6$, so $P=1$ (lifted points are generically still in general position).

lec05kp14-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp14-u01-p6-c3.text: **Simulation** (1500 runs): 0.494 for the original two dimensions and 1.000 for the quadratic features.

lec05kp14-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp14-u01-p7-title.text: 100 points with random labels: exactly half at l=49 and 98.7% separable at l=60

lec05kp14-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p7-bridge.text: Lifting raised the probability of separable random labels from 0.49 to 1. With 100 samples, how many dimensions are enough?

lec05kp14-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-need
lec05kp14-u01-p7-fig1.text: S-shaped curve of the probability of separable against dimension l for N=100: 0.035 at l=40, exactly 0.5 at l=49 and 0.987 at l=60.

image.alt: S-shaped curve of the probability of separable against dimension l for N=100: 0.035 at l=40, exactly 0.5 at l=49 and 0.987 at l=60.

lec05kp14-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p7-c1.text: **Rule**: for $N>l+1$ some labelings fail; once the data exceed twice the degrees of freedom ($l+1$ adjustable parameters), $N>2(l+1)$, the probability of separable drops below half.

lec05kp14-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp14-u01-p7-c3.text: **Meaning**: to separate random labels by lifting, the dimension must reach about half the number of samples or more.

lec05kp14-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp14-u01-p8-title.text: Lifting raises separability, not generalization: new points are only 50% right

lec05kp14-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p8-bridge.text: At 60 dimensions 100 points with random labels are 98.7% separable. Does separable mean new data are also classified correctly?

lec05kp14-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp14-gen
lec05kp14-u01-p8-fig1.text: Random-label experiment: the 5 training points are 100% right while 200 new points are only 50.4% right.

image.alt: Random-label experiment: the 5 training points are 100% right while 200 new points are only 50.4% right.

lec05kp14-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p8-c1.text: **Experiment** (designed here): 5 two-dimensional Gaussian points with random labels, a separating hyperplane in the quadratic features (5 dimensions): found in all 300 runs, training all right.

lec05kp14-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp14-u01-p8-c2.text: **New data**: 200 fresh points with random labels are only 50.4% right on average, which is guessing.

lec05kp14-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp14-u01-p8-c3.text: **So**: lifting only guarantees that the training data can be separated; only data with a pattern can be learned, and generalization is a separate matter (Chapter 5).

lec05kp14-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp14-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: why the critical probability is exactly 1/2: the symmetry of binomial coefficients

lec05kp14-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p9-bridge.text: Lifting only guarantees separability, and the probability of separable is exactly $1/2$ at $r=2$. Is that a coincidence?

lec05kp14-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp14-u01-p9-c1.text: **Symmetry**: at the critical $N=2l+2$, $N-1=2l+1$ is odd and $\binom{2l+1}{i}=\binom{2l+1}{2l+1-i}$, so the sum over $i\le l$ is exactly half of the total $2^{2l+1}$, namely $2^{2l}$.

lec05kp14-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp14-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, O and P for N=5 points

lec05kp14-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p10-bridge.text: The critical probability is exactly one half thanks to the symmetry of binomial coefficients. Take $N=5$ points: what are $O$ and the probability of separable, and what about 3 dimensions?

lec05kp14-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp14-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp14-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp14-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked what are $O$ and the probability of separable for $N=5$ points. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp14-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp14-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the 22 for $N=5$ matches the table of page 2; one more dimension raises the probability of separable from 0.6875 to 0.9375.

steps.label: Cover's theorem
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The formula and the critical point N=2(l+1) follow the source; every number (14 against 16, the probability table, the Monte Carlo 0.865 and 0.503, the lifting 0.494 against 1.000, the N=100 table, the random-label generalization experiment) was recomputed by a program, and the Monte Carlo and generalization experiments were designed for this lecture (added). Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: How many splits
steps.speakerNotes: KP13 lifted the data to new coordinates and then used a straight line. This page asks whether lifting really helps. First count: into how many two-class splits can one line cut some points? One word first: a dichotomy is one way of labeling N points with two classes, and the ones a line can realize are the linear dichotomies. With three points all 8 labelings are separable by a line; with four points at the corners of a square, 14 of the 16 labelings are separable and the 2 that are not put the diagonal pairs together, which are XOR and XNOR, as a program checked one by one over all 16. The next page asks whether we can compute the count directly instead of counting one by one.

steps.label: The counting formula
steps.speakerNotes: On the previous page one line got 14 splits of four points and 2 were missing. This page asks whether we can compute the count directly. One word first: general position means points in l dimensions with no l plus 1 of them on one hyperplane of l minus 1 dimensions; in two dimensions, no three on a line. Cover's formula: O equals 2 times the sum over i from 0 to l of N minus 1 choose i. Check: N equal to 4 and l equal to 2 gives 2 times 1 plus 3 plus 3, which is 14; N equal to 3 gives 2 times 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 8, equal to 2 to the 3. For N at most l plus 1, O equals 2 to the N, so all labelings are separable. In the table O is 2, 4, 8, 14, 22, 32, 44 and 58 while 2 to the N is 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256. The next page asks the probability of separable when the labels are random.

steps.label: Probability of separable
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said all labelings are separable while N is at most l plus 1 and that some go missing beyond that. This page asks the probability of separable when the labels are random. The probability P is O over 2 to the N, and it is 1 while N is at most l plus 1. In two dimensions, for N from 1 to 10, it is 1, 1, 1, 0.875, 0.6875, 0.5, 0.344, 0.227, 0.145 and 0.090. Once N passes 3 the probability starts to fall and it reaches exactly half at N equal to 6. The next page asks where that half appears in other dimensions.

steps.label: The phase transition
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that N equal to 6 in two dimensions gives exactly half. This page asks where that half appears in other dimensions. One word first: a phase transition means the turn of the probability from 1 down to 0 gets sharper as the dimension grows, like water freezing. Write N as r times l plus 1 and plot the probability against r: every dimension's curve passes through (2, 1/2) because at N equal to 2 times l plus 1, O equals 2 to the 2l plus 1, which I checked for l from 1 to 7. The higher the dimension the steeper: at r equal to 1.5 and 2.5 the probabilities are 0.75 and 0.31 for l equal to 1, 0.97 and 0.08 for l equal to 19 and 1.00 and 0.0007 for l equal to 99. The next page asks whether random points and labels really give these numbers.

steps.label: A random test
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the probability at the critical point r equal to 2 is one half. This page asks whether random points with random labels give the same numbers. Each run draws N two-dimensional Gaussian points with random plus or minus 1 labels and uses a linear program to decide whether a separating line exists, 1500 runs each. The results are 0.865 at N equal to 4 against 0.875 from the formula and 0.503 at N equal to 6 against 0.500. With 1500 runs the standard error is about 0.01, so the gap is about one standard error. The formula and the simulation agree. The next page asks what lifting the same points does.

steps.label: The effect of lifting
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the simulation matches the formula: N equal to 6 in two dimensions is only 0.5. This page asks what happens to the same points after lifting. With the same random points and labels, x1 and x2 alone is l equal to 2; adding x1 squared, x2 squared and x1 times x2 makes l equal to 5. The formula predicts that N equal to 6 is at most l plus 1 equal to 6, so P equals 1. The simulation over 1500 runs gives 0.494 for the original two dimensions and 1.000 for the quadratic features. The next page asks how many dimensions are enough for 100 samples.

steps.label: How many dimensions
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed lifting raised the probability from 0.49 to 1. This page asks how many dimensions are enough with 100 samples. The rule is that once the data exceed twice the degrees of freedom, that is N above 2 times l plus 1, separability starts to fail. For N equal to 100: l equal to 40 gives 0.035, 48 gives 0.42, 49 gives exactly 0.5, 56 gives 0.92, 60 gives 0.987 and 68 gives 0.9999. The meaning is that to separate random labels by lifting, the dimension must reach about half the number of samples or more. The next page asks whether being separable means new data are classified correctly.

steps.label: Separable is not general
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that at 60 dimensions 100 points with random labels are 98.7% separable. This page asks whether separable means new data are classified correctly. The experiment was designed here: 5 two-dimensional Gaussian points with random labels, a separating hyperplane found in the quadratic features, which is 5 dimensions, in all 300 runs with training all right; then 200 fresh points, also with random labels, are only 50.4% right on average, which is guessing. So lifting only guarantees that the training data can be separated; only data with a pattern can be learned, and generalization is a separate matter that Chapter 5 returns to. The next extension page looks at why the critical point is exactly one half.

steps.label: Extension: why half
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said lifting only guarantees separability. This extension asks whether it is a coincidence that the probability of separable is exactly one half at r equal to 2. It is not; it follows from the symmetry of binomial coefficients: 2l plus 1 choose i equals 2l plus 1 choose 2l plus 1 minus i, so the sum over i at most l is exactly half of the total 2 to the 2l plus 1, namely 2 to the 2l. So O equals 2 times 2 to the 2l, which is 2 to the 2l plus 1, and P is one half. Check: for l from 1 to 5, O is 8, 32, 128, 512 and 2048. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the critical probability is exactly one half thanks to the symmetry of binomial coefficients. This page poses an exercise with N equal to 5 points. Question 1: what are O and the probability of separable P for l equal to 2? The hint is that O is 2 times the sum of N minus 1 choose i, and 4 choose i is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. Question 2: lifting to l equal to 3, what is P? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: O(5, 2) is 2 times 1 plus 4 plus 6, which is 22, and P is 22 over 32, which is 0.6875. Question 2: O(5, 3) is 2 times 1 plus 4 plus 6 plus 4, which is 30, and P is 30 over 32, which is 0.9375. Check: the 22 for N equal to 5 matches the table of page 2, and one more dimension raises the probability of separable from 0.6875 to 0.9375. That finishes Cover's theorem; the next knowledge point looks at polynomial classifiers: very capable, at a startling price.
